extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers, experimental investigators, and students of inductive method (Baconian science)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on selecting and using special classes of empirical instances (the 'prerogative instances') to conduct true induction and discover forms/natures in natural philosophy. Includes the distinction between true/formal and operative definitions and a taxonomy of ten ranks of high‑value instances with examples and cautions.

rubrics_metrics.name: True (formal) vs. operative definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguishes the 'form or true definition' (considered relatively to the universe, not the senses) from the 'operative definition' (definition considered relatively to experiments and the senses). Example: heat defined as 'an expansive motion restrained, and striving to exert itself in the smaller particles.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: True/formal definition: seek the underlying motion or form that constitutes the nature across bodies (not only sensory appearances). Operative definition: demonstrate the phenomenon by producing the underlying motion experimentally (e.g., excite a dilating motion and repress it to produce heat). Both views are necessary: the true definition for understanding, the operative for experimental verification and application. Sensible (perceptual) definitions should be related back to the true/formal definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of prerogative instances (overall)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prerogative instances are special kinds of examples that accelerate and confirm induction; Bacon enumerates ranks of such instances as essential 'helps of the understanding' in true and perfect induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodological outline: after initial tables (first review, exclusive table, first vintage), investigators should employ prerogative instances along with supports and corrections of induction, vary investigation by subject, consider prerogative natures (which to research first/last), set limits of investigation (synopsis of natures), apply to practical purposes, prepare investigations, and use axiom scales. The prerogative instances themselves are to be chosen and applied according to their rank and purpose (see individual ranks).

rubrics_metrics.name: Solitary instances (wild/solitary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances that exhibit the required nature in subjects that have nothing in common with others except that nature, or that fail to exhibit the nature in subjects resembling others except in the nature in question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use solitary instances because 'a few of them are of as much avail as many'—they remove prolixity and accelerate exclusion. Examples: prisms and dews for color (they share color but nothing else with fixed colors); veins of white and black in marble show color independent of intrinsic nature. Solitary instances help deduce that a property depends on a particular cause (e.g., texture, incidence of light).

rubrics_metrics.name: Migrating instances
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances in which the required nature passes toward generation (coming into being) or toward corruption (passing away), or toward increase or decrease—i.e., the nature is observed in the process of change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Migrating instances 'hasten and confirm exclusion' and narrow the candidate form because they show what is added or removed when the nature appears/disappears. Useful for identifying what conveys or destroys the form. Example: powdered glass (white) vs. whole glass (transparent) shows whiteness arises from division of parts and inclusion of air. Caution: do not over-attribute the form to efficient causes (e.g., erroneously concluding air is always necessary for whiteness); remedy by systematic exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conspicuous (coruscations / free and predominant) instances
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances that show the required nature in its bare substantial shape and at its greatest degree of power, emancipated from impediments—i.e., clear, predominant manifestations of the nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conspicuous instances are valuable because they reveal the form strongly (example: thermometer for the expansive motion of heat; quicksilver for weight). But beware: whatever merely 'makes a show' of the form or forces it forward is suspect; always apply severe and diligent exclusion to ensure the conspicuous instance reveals the true form and not an artifact or efficient that masks the real nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clandestine (twilight) instances
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances that show the required nature in its lowest state or rudiments, concealed and subdued by a contrary nature—small or faint manifestations that reveal the underlying tendency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clandestine instances are crucial for leading to genera rather than differences; they often appear in small portions of bodies (e.g., water bubbles, threads of eaves' droppings, froth and snow showing consistency in fluids). Use these to discover latent tendencies (e.g., cohesion, tendency to avoid breach of continuity). Examine small-scale or weak examples to reveal the germ of a nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutive (collective) instances
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances that constitute a species or lesser form of the required nature; groups of instances that collect into a common notion and assist in forming preliminary definitions and divisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track particular groups of instances that consistently unite to produce a recognizable subform (e.g., aids to memory: order, commonplaces, verse). These 'lesser forms' help in constructing definitions, partitions, and the division of a nature. But avoid stopping at these partial partitions—continue investigation to seek the greater or leading form that unites more fully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Similar or proportionate instances (physical parallels)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances that exhibit resemblances and connections of things in the concrete, showing physical parallels across different domains (analogies grounded in substantive resemblance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use similar instances to map the frame and anatomy of parts of the universe and to rise to axioms about construction (e.g., mirror and eye; ear and echo; roots and branches). They are especially helpful for higher axioms about the world's construction rather than simple natures. Caution: restrict to real, substantial resemblances, not superficial or superstitious sympathies (avoid the 'natural magic' style of fanciful analogies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Singular (heteroclite) instances
rubrics_metrics.description: Irregular or extraordinary instances that exhibit a subject as extravagant or separate from its species—rare cases that do not agree much with others of the same species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Singular instances are like clandestine ones in that they provoke inquiry and can unite nature by showing exceptional combinations; investigate them until their properties reduce to some form or law. Examples: sun and moon among heavenly bodies, magnet among minerals, quicksilver among metals. Treat them as valuable correctives to habit and useful for keeping inquiry alive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deviating instances (errors of nature / monsters)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances showing deviations or errors of nature—monstrous or prodigious individuals that depart from ordinary course; they differ from singular instances (which are miraculous at species level) by being miracles of individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use deviant instances to rectify understanding opposed to habit and to reveal latent processes toward forms. They are often especially useful for practical/artificial application (easier to vary known species than generate new ones). Collect such monsters and anomalies systematically and critically, using rigorous selection and credible sources (avoid superstition and untrustworthy reports).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bordering instances (participants)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances that exhibit species appearing to be composed of two species or intermediate between two species—those that lie on the boundary between types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bordering instances point out order and constitution of things and suggest causes for species numbers and qualities; they lead the understanding from existing species to what is possible (examples: moss between putrescence and plant; flying fishes between fish and bird; bats between birds and quadrupeds). Treat them as rare but informative for classification and the study of transitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instances of power (fasces / masterpieces)
rubrics_metrics.description: Works or operations that are most noble and perfect—masterpieces of art and achievement that display human power over nature and from which new discoveries or applications are easiest derived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study perfect works of art and technology as 'instances of power' because they elevate the understanding and make transitions to new, undiscovered works easier (the mode of effecting art is often plain compared to nature's obscurity). Use them both to inspire and to guide practical application of natural forms to human ends; enumerate and examine the most polished and perfected works in each art.
